title: Shishupala
hook: Shishupala challenges Krishna to fight, and Krishna finally speaks: the pardons are used up
carry: name your limit, kindly and clearly

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bhishma told of Shishupala's birth, and Krishna's promise to his aunt: a hundred pardons. Your line was his silence is a promise kept. Did you keep one small promise, even at a cost? Day seven hundred sixty-two.

Bhishma's story should have cooled the room. It does the opposite. Shishupala hears that he's been spared all his life by Krishna's promise, and he's not grateful. He's insulted. He turns from Bhishma to Krishna himself and calls him out: stand up and fight me. For the first time in this whole scene, the challenge is aimed straight at the silent guest. Every king in the hall is watching. Today, after all that waiting, Krishna speaks.
screen: `THE STORY DOESN'T COOL HIM.` → `FIGHT ME.` → `THE SILENT GUEST STANDS.`

segments.voice: Krishna doesn't answer Shishupala first. He turns to the kings. In the telling, he lays out what Shishupala has done in the past: wrongs done against Krishna's own people, some of them while Krishna was far away and couldn't defend them. He reminds the hall that Shishupala is his aunt's son, and that for her sake he has borne all of this. And then he says the line the whole week has been waiting for, in effect: the hundred are full. The promise has been kept to the end. Shishupala doesn't back down. He laughs at Krishna and dares him to do his worst. So Krishna calls to mind his discus, the spinning weapon that is his in the stories, and it comes to his hand. And in front of all the kings, he strikes, and the king of Chedi falls. Sit with how this happens, because the order matters. Krishna doesn't strike at the first insult, or the tenth. He doesn't strike when Bhima wants to. He waits until his word to his aunt has been fully kept. And even then, before he acts, he explains himself to the room. The poem shows patience and judgment as two parts of the same thing. Patience isn't endless here. It has a shape and a limit, and the limit was set long ago, in love, for a frightened mother. Some readers find the ending hard. Some find it just. The poem gives us the waiting, the warning and the blow, and lets us hold all three.
screen: `KRISHNA SPEAKS TO THE KINGS.` · `FOR HIS AUNT'S SAKE, HE BORE IT.` · `THE HUNDRED ARE FULL.` · `THE DISCUS COMES TO HIS HAND.` · then, large: `PATIENCE WITH A SHAPE AND A LIMIT.`

segments.voice: Let the breath settle low in the belly. Bring to mind a situation where you've been patient for a long time, maybe with a person, maybe with a habit of your own. Ask yourself quietly: where is the limit here? You don't have to decide anything now. Just notice whether there's a line, and whether you know where it is. Breathe in steadiness. Breathe out the strain of waiting. If you pray, you can ask in your prayer for clarity about it. If not, rest with the question. The bell holds the time.
Shishupala. The king who challenged Krishna once too often, after a hundred pardons kept for his mother's sake had run out.
Your line: name your limit, kindly and clearly. Today, if you've been patient with something for a long time, name your limit to yourself, kindly and clearly. Day seven hundred sixty-two.

howItsDone: In Hindu retellings and devotional art, the Sudarshana discus is one of Krishna's signs, and some tellers present the end of Shishupala as the moment his long patience reaches its promised limit.

match.prompt: the end in the hall — tap the pairs.

myth: Krishna struck at Shishupala's first insult
he waited until the hundred pardons promised to his aunt were full.
Krishna explained himself to the kings before he acted
he named Shishupala's past wrongs and his promise before he struck.
Bhima was the one who killed Shishupala
Bhishma held Bhima back; it was Krishna, with his discus.

fork.setup: you're Krishna. Shishupala has used up every pardon you promised his mother, and now he dares you to fight. what do you do first?
fork.reveal: Krishna first tells the kings what Shishupala has done and why he bore it, and only then calls his discus.

original.note: Sanskrit cakra: wheel or discus; Krishna's discus comes to his hand at the end of the scene.

trapdoor: what you thought: Krishna finally lost his temper.
what it means: he waited until his promise of a hundred pardons was fully kept, then explained himself and acted.
what a scholar hears: the scene joins patience and judgment, with the limit fixed long before by a promise to a mother.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva, Sisupala-badha Parva (Shishupala challenges Krishna; Krishna addresses the kings, recounts his offenses and his promise; the discus)

notes: All paraphrase. Confirm that Krishna addresses the kings and lists Shishupala's past wrongs against the Yadavas, some committed while Krishna was away; the specific wrongs are deliberately not named.
Confirm Krishna says, in sense, that the pardons promised to his aunt are now exhausted, and that Shishupala laughs and taunts him.
Confirm the discus comes to Krishna's hand when he thinks of it.
The death is described briefly and without gore on purpose.
howItsDone names the discus as Sudarshana and calls it one of Krishna's signs; the spoken script does not use the name. Confirm.
Editor pass: softened howItsDone 'is often told' to 'some tellers present'; spoken script unchanged.
Audit (2026-10-01): checked that Krishna addresses the kings first, names past wrongs done while he was away, and calls the discus to mind; no change needed.
